output.situation: The user freelances and says some months are great while others are almost empty, and they want to budget without knowing what they will earn. The tension is between planning around a typical income and protecting against the worst stretch. The decisive unknown, which the user has not given, is how low the emptiest months go, how long they last in a row, and whether fixed bills fit under them.

minds.title: The Income Smoother
minds.concern: Spending should follow what you can sustainably earn over a long stretch, not what happened to arrive this month.
minds.author: Milton Friedman
minds.book: A Theory of the Consumption Function

minds.title: The Barbell Builder
minds.concern: Protect against the worst realistic stretch and keep the freedom to say no, so one bad run cannot break you.
minds.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

minds.title: The Reserve Keeper
minds.concern: Build a habit that moves money out of reach before it can be spent, so the plan does not depend on forecasting or willpower.
minds.author: George S. Clason

debate.speaker: The Income Smoother
debate.text: The user is treating each month as its own paycheck, and that is what makes the empty ones feel like emergencies. I read this as a measuring problem before a budgeting problem. What you can safely spend is set by what you earn over a long stretch, not by the deposit that landed this month.
debate.author: Milton Friedman
debate.book: A Theory of the Consumption Function
debate.basis: [Basis: Milton Friedman, A Theory of the Consumption Function, the permanent income idea (paraphrased from the book's well-known argument; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Barbell Builder
debate.text: Measuring over a long stretch is the trap, because an average hides the bad stretch that actually breaks you. When live events shut down in 2020, stagehands and touring musicians went months near zero, and no yearly average paid their rent. Set the baseline by a realistic worst month and treat everything above it as a bonus.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: [Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, the barbell strategy and fragility (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Reserve Keeper
debate.text: You are both arguing about the number and skipping the habit, and the great months are where this is won. Move a fixed share of every deposit into a separate account before spending anything, then draw a steady amount from it. I would go further than the book and save a bigger share when money is plentiful, since that is when it is painless.
debate.author: George S. Clason
debate.basis: [Basis: George S. Clason, The Richest Man in Babylon, the idea of paying yourself first (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Income Smoother
debate.text: The 2020 shutdown is a fair hit, because my average would have overstated what a stagehand could safely spend. I change my position: draw from the lower end of recent months, not the mean, and treat the rest as a top-up. I keep one point, though. A baseline set by the single worst month would starve a perfectly healthy year.
debate.author: Milton Friedman
debate.book: A Theory of the Consumption Function
debate.basis: [Basis: Milton Friedman, A Theory of the Consumption Function, the permanent income idea (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Barbell Builder
debate.text: The user wrote that some months are almost empty. That may mean the empty months, more than the uncertainty itself, are what weigh on them. My guess is that worry like that pushes people to accept any client. If so, what matters is a cushion that lets them turn a bad job down. That is my own extension of the book.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: [Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, optionality (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Reserve Keeper
debate.text: I would not assume it is the empty months. They also wrote that they do not know what they will earn, which may mean deciding everything again each month. They may want to spend freely when money is high and feel safe when it is thin, and they cannot fully have both. A fixed draw buys the calm. Spending the surplus buys the freedom.
debate.author: George S. Clason
debate.basis: [Basis: George S. Clason, The Richest Man in Babylon, the idea of paying yourself first (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Income Smoother
debate.text: All of this turns on a fact the user has not given: do their fixed bills fit under their lowest months, and how many empty months come in a row? If the bills fit, I favour a steady draw with a small buffer. If they do not, the barbell wins, because no smoothing helps when the floor sits below the rent. Cutting fixed costs comes first.
debate.author: Milton Friedman
debate.book: A Theory of the Consumption Function
debate.basis: [Basis: Milton Friedman, A Theory of the Consumption Function, the permanent income idea (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Barbell Builder
debate.text: Notice what is lost if the floor sits under the rent: bargaining power, not just money. After the 2008 crash, work dried up for many architects, and my guess is that some took any project at any fee. If anyone depends on the user, they are exposed too. If that is the real concern, the buffer size in months matters more than any savings percentage.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: [Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, fragility and optionality (paraphrased; the 2008 example is my own illustration, not the author's; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Reserve Keeper
debate.text: The user wrote that some months are great. That may mean the great months feel like permission to spend, which would make the empty ones hurt more. If so, the fix is not a smarter forecast but moving the money before it is visible. Smoother, your lower-end draw still lets a spender spend the surplus.
debate.author: George S. Clason
debate.basis: [Basis: George S. Clason, The Richest Man in Babylon, the idea of paying yourself first (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Income Smoother
debate.text: I would not make that the default reading. Great months can be slow catch-up, when late invoices finally land and get spent on bills already overdue. The 2023 Hollywood writers strike showed how a long gap hits even steady earners. So check payment timing first. If timing is the cause, a buffer of one invoice cycle does more than a savings share.
debate.author: Milton Friedman
debate.book: A Theory of the Consumption Function
debate.basis: [Basis: Milton Friedman, A Theory of the Consumption Function, income smoothing over time (paraphrased; the strike example is my own illustration, not the author's; source link not verified)]

debate.speaker: The Barbell Builder
debate.text: We still disagree on the baseline. Smoother wants the lower end of recent months, and I want the worst realistic month. The user own history would decide it: how low the emptiest months went, how many came in a row, and whether the bills fit underneath. A short, shallow dip favours Smoother. A long, deep one favours me.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
debate.basis: [Basis: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile, the barbell strategy (paraphrased; source link not verified)]

output.clearer: The main insight is that the question splits in two: which number to live on, and what to do with the money in good months. The minds moved toward a baseline below the average, drawn from a separate reserve. They still dispute how low that baseline should sit, and whether the real danger is the empty months, the late payments, or the pull to spend in good months. One possible self-reflection: when a month is empty, does it feel more like a money problem or a decision problem, and does that change which rule would help?
output.dependsOn:
- If the fixed bills fit under the lowest months and the dips are short, a steady draw from the lower end of recent months, with a small buffer, becomes more reasonable. The shortfall is then modest and smoothing covers it.
- If the fixed bills sit above the lowest months, or empty stretches run long, a baseline set by the worst realistic month and a buffer counted in months of fixed costs becomes more reasonable. Cutting fixed costs comes first, because smoothing cannot fill a gap that deep.
- If late payments explain many of the empty months, a buffer of roughly one invoice cycle is the better first step.
- If the user tends to spend whatever a good month brings, moving a fixed share into a separate account before spending becomes more reasonable.
- The decisive unknown is the user's own record. A proportionate way to learn it is to list the last twelve months of income against fixed bills, noting the lowest month and the longest low run.
